48.0.0.en: 1- Great is the LORD, and greatly to be praised in the city of our God, in the mountain of his holiness.

48.0.1.en: 1- The writer first glorifies the builder of the city, who is God, and describes Him as great and worthy of praise and thanksgiving for His care and keeping of His children, and for all His great and good works.

48.0.2.en: 2- He describes Jerusalem and names it the mountain of God's holiness, since it is built on five mountains and in it is His holy Temple. He also describes it as the city of our God in which He dwells and which He blesses, and this means the special relationship with God, for He is our God, and the beauty of God appears in the greatness of His city and in His Temple. And the mountain of God's holiness, by the spirit of prophecy, is the Church, and the soul of every believer.

48.1.0.en: 2- Beautiful for situation, the joy of the whole earth, is mount Zion, on the sides of the north, the city of the great King.

48.1.1.en: The writer speaks about the attributes of the city of God, and describes it as follows:

48.1.2.en: 1- Beautiful for situation: it is elevated because it is built on mountains, and this elevation is beautiful, not only because it draws the eyes of people to its great Temple, but also because it is a type of its being raised above earthly and material things, and its drawing near to heavenly things, for it represents holiness, spirituality and loftiness.

48.1.3.en: 2- The joy of the whole earth: it gladdens the hearts of all who believe in God in all the earth, who come to worship in His holy Temple, and from it Christ would come, the joy and salvation of all the earth.

48.1.4.en: 3- Mount Zion: it is firm like the mountain, strong like Mount Zion on which it is built, because God establishes it by His dwelling in it.

48.1.5.en: 4- The joy of the sides of the north: it is the joy and salvation of the pagan great ones who come from the north, namely the Assyrians, the Babylonians and Persia, who attacked Jerusalem. These believed in Christ who came forth from Jerusalem, and submitted to Him and rejoiced in His salvation.

48.1.6.en: 5- The city of the great King: it is the dwelling place of God the great King, because He dwells in Jerusalem His city and gladdens it with His blessings.

48.1.7.en: These five attributes are enjoyed by every soul that has believed in Christ and in which He dwells: she is lofty, joyful and firm, her heart is open to all, and she enjoys the dwelling of Christ in her.

48.2.0.en: 3- God is known in her palaces for a refuge.

48.2.1.en: 1- The palaces of the city of God are its great buildings which God blesses, so that they become a refuge for its inhabitants, who take shelter in them because God is with them. This is what happened to Jerusalem as long as she was firm in her faith, but when she forsook God and worshipped idols the Babylonians destroyed her.

48.2.2.en: 2- The palaces are the souls of the believers in which God dwells, so that they become a refuge to which all people take shelter, to take of their peace and joy, and to learn from them how to live with God. So she is a refuge for them in the midst of the wilderness of the world.

48.2.3.en: God wants to beautify your soul, and raise it above the world so that it may be a light to every person; so submit to Him and hold fast to His commandments, that He may dwell in you, satisfy you, gladden you and work through you.

48.3.0.en: 4- For, lo, the kings were assembled, they passed by together. 5- They saw it, and so they marvelled; they were troubled, and hasted away. 6- Fear took hold upon them there, and pain, as of a woman in travail. 7- Thou breakest the ships of Tarshish with an east wind.

48.3.1.en: Tarshish: a famous commercial city in the ancient world, located in the south of Spain.

48.3.2.en: 1- The writer of the psalm tells us about the assembling of kings to attack the city of God, Jerusalem, but strangely, after their assembling they departed and could not harm the city. Why was that? He declares the reason, which is that these kings saw something that amazed them, so they marvelled greatly, then feared with a great fear, and fled quickly. They felt terrible dread, and even suffered from their fear as a woman suffers when she is giving birth, as the pains of travail come upon her suddenly; thus they suffered intensely and fled far away. The sudden, intense terror of these enemies is likened to what happens when a strong east wind blows upon the great ships of Tarshish and breaks and ruins them.

48.3.3.en: 2- This did in fact happen more than once with the city of Jerusalem. The kings of Moab, Edom and the children of Ammon assembled to attack Jerusalem in the days of King Jehoshaphat, who prayed to God and He reassured him; and Jehoshaphat went out with his army with the companies of praisers at the head of it, and when the allied armies of the enemies saw them they were struck dumb and marvelled greatly at this praise, but they were seized with great fear when a group of soldiers who had been hiding in ambushes rose up against them, and panic covered them and they fled. Perhaps these ambushes were angelic soldiers (2 Chr 20:22). It also happened when the commanders of the Assyrian armies assembled and besieged Jerusalem under the leadership of Sennacherib in the days of Hezekiah king of Judah, who prayed to God, and Isaiah the prophet reassured him. And in the night the angel of the LORD appeared with his drawn sword to the armies of the Assyrians, and they were struck dumb, then feared greatly, especially when the sword of the angel began to work upon their necks, so that 185,000 soldiers of the enemy armies fell, and the rest fled (2 Kgs 19:35).

48.3.4.en: 3- These verses show that however great the power of the enemies, and their pride and greatness, like the ships of Tarshish, God, when He sees them wishing to harm His city Jerusalem, frightens them, so they are troubled, and suffer, and flee. And the east wind is a type of the Holy Spirit, who shatters the power of the unbelievers who attack the city of God, and even turns some of them to faith, while the rest flee in great fear.

48.4.0.en: 8- As we have heard, so have we seen in the city of the LORD of hosts, in the city of our God: God will establish it for ever. Selah.

48.4.1.en: 1- The writer declares that God's protection of His city was fulfilled in the days of the fathers, and we heard of it from them, such as the ten plagues in Egypt, the crossing of the Red Sea, and also the parting of the Jordan, the crossing of the people of God, the fall of the walls of Jericho, and all the victories of God in the land of Canaan. In addition to this the writer says we have seen with our own eyes the works of God, and His protection of His children in our generation, for the works of God are renewed every day, for He is "the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever" (Heb 13:8). And He is the Lord of the invincible heavenly hosts, and He protects His city and establishes it for ever. What is meant by being established for ever is the heavenly Jerusalem, where the children of God reign with Him forever; for the earthly Jerusalem was destroyed more than once, but that which is established for ever is the heavenly Jerusalem.

48.4.2.en: 2- At the end of the verse is the word Selah, which is a musical pause for contemplating the greatness of the city of God, and His mighty work in her, that we may glorify Him and praise Him.

48.4.3.en: Believe in God and hold fast to His commandments however much troubles or threats surround you; they cannot harm you, and God keeps you and establishes your faith, until He transfers you to heaven and gives you joy with Him in His Kingdom.

48.5.0.en: 9- We have thought of thy lovingkindness, O God, in the midst of thy temple. 10- According to thy name, O God, so is thy praise unto the ends of the earth: thy right hand is full of righteousness.

48.5.1.en: 1- After we heard and saw the greatness of God in (v. 8), now in this verse we remember and speak of His great works.

48.5.2.en: 2- Being in the Temple of God makes us feel His presence, and makes us remember Him, and remember His mercy and His great works. Just as His name is holy, so all His works are holy, and great, and good. And the highest form of God's mercy appears in His condescending to give us His Body and Blood on the altar every day for forgiveness, comfort and satisfaction of His children.

48.5.3.en: 3- It is the nature of God to do righteousness, and His right hand, that is, His power, appears in the abundance of His righteousness. And the greatest form of His right hand is the Incarnation of His only-begotten Son Jesus Christ to redeem mankind and fill the world with righteousness by His good works. All this makes those who believe in God praise Him continually.

48.6.0.en: 11- Let mount Zion rejoice, let the daughters of Judah be glad, because of thy judgments.

48.6.1.en: God, who governs the world by His wisdom, created all things and set for them laws by which they proceed, in addition to His commandments and judgments, which He gave to His children to live by, leading them to the Kingdom. In all this His city Zion rejoices, that is, Jerusalem, established by His power like the mountain, and she is a type of the firm Church of the New Testament and of the heavenly Jerusalem, firm forever; and the daughters of Judah who worship God in Jerusalem also rejoice, and they are a type of the souls of those who believe in God, for they rejoice in His presence in their midst, and in His judgments and commandments which guide them on their way.

48.6.2.en: God calls you to joy if you meditate on His commandments and His word, so be satisfied with the Holy Bible every day, and praise His holy name, and your heart will be filled with peace.

48.7.0.en: 12- Walk about Zion, and go round about her: tell the towers thereof. 13- Mark ye well her bulwarks, consider her palaces; that ye may tell it to the generation following.

48.7.1.en: 1- Zion is the most important of the mountains on which the city of Jerusalem is built, so the writer calls the believers to walk about and go round the city, to contemplate its beauty and see its firmness. This was a custom of the ancients after the end of a war, to make sure of the soundness of the city's walls and towers; and by this going about they discovered the power of God and His protection and glorified Him, just as a person needs to go round his life and contemplate it after every spiritual battle, that is, to examine himself, to be reassured of his safety from any evil, and to glorify God who brought him through the trial.

48.7.2.en: 2- The towers are the places of watching during war to protect the city from the enemies, the bulwarks are the walls built for the inhabitants to take shelter behind, and the palaces are the greatest buildings within the city. The towers are a type of the saints, the bulwarks a type of the means of grace, and the palaces a type of the virtues with which the Church and every believer are adorned. Therefore every person should examine himself, and how firmly he holds to holiness and the means of grace, and his striving to acquire virtues, and thank God for all His blessings, and tell of them to his children, that they may be firm in the faith and enjoy the work of God in the Church.

48.8.0.en: 14- For this God is our God for ever and ever: he will be our guide even unto death. At the close of the psalm the writer declares an important truth, which is that God, who founded and preserved this city and its Temple, is our God whom we worship with all our hearts, especially since He walks with us on the way of life, and guides us to the Kingdom all our lives until death, and even continues with us in the Kingdom forever, to give us joy in His fellowship.

48.8.1.en: May you examine yourself every day, to know how often the enemy made you fall into sin, and how God kept you from many evils, and review how active you are in striving toward virtue, that you may be fortified in it. And as God sees your concern He supports you, blesses you and establishes you.

48.8.2.en: The inevitability of death. To the chief musician. For the sons of Korah. A psalm: "Hear this, all ye people") ... v. 1) Introduction:

48.8.3.en: 1- Its writer: the sons of Korah.

48.8.4.en: 2- A wisdom psalm, that is, one full of words of wisdom, resembling the books of Job, Proverbs, Wisdom, and Jesus the son of Sirach.

48.8.5.en: 3- It clarifies an important idea, which is that the rich who are great in the earth are not better than the poor, because the end of all of them is one, which is death.

48.8.6.en: 4- Many wise sayings and counsels are drawn from this psalm, the most important of which are:

48.8.7.en: a- The importance of uprightness in life.

48.8.9.en: c- The strangeness of the world (our being strangers in it).

48.8.10.en: 5- This psalm is the eighth of the psalms which bear the title "for the sons of Korah," which are the psalms (Ps 42-49), to which four other psalms for the sons of Korah are added, namely (Ps 84, 85, 87, 88), so that the total of the psalms bearing "for the sons of Korah" in their titles is twelve psalms.

48.8.11.en: 6- This psalm is not found in the Agpeya.

49.0.s.en: (1) A call to all to listen

49.0.0.en: 1- Hear this, all ye people; give ear, all ye inhabitants of the world:

49.0.1.en: The writer calls all peoples and those who dwell in the world, whether great or lowly, rich or poor, that is, all peoples, including the Jews, to hear and listen attentively to the truths he will mention in this psalm. By this he shows the importance of what he is about to say.

49.1.0.en: 3- My mouth shall speak of wisdom; and the meditation of my heart shall be of understanding. 4- I will incline mine ear to a parable: I will open my dark saying upon the harp. Meditation of my heart: recurring feelings that take hold and dominate.

49.1.1.en: I will incline mine ear: I will listen humbly.

49.1.2.en: 1- The writer makes clear that what he declares in this psalm is wisdom and counsel uttered by his tongue, springing from feelings that recur within him. He feels every word he speaks, because they are important truths and basic concepts that every person needs.

49.1.3.en: 2- The writer also humbles himself, listening to the beating of his heart, and then expresses it in a parable that confirms the truth he wants, because parables affect the hearer more than the direct truth, and are easy to understand. He also explains the counsels he declares, which seem hidden like a riddle, and presents them set to music, accompanied by a musical instrument, the harp, so that the hearer may accept them more easily.

49.1.4.en: May you listen attentively to the words of God and the guidance of your father of confession, for they are the direct voice of God to you, to act on, so that you live reassured and take steady steps toward the Kingdom.

49.2.s.en: (2) Death, the end of all men

49.2.0.en: 5- Wherefore should I fear in the days of evil, when the iniquity of my heels shall compass me about?

49.2.1.en: My heels: that is, my two heels, which are the two heel bones at the bottom of a person's feet.

49.2.2.en: 1- The writer asks why I should fear the days of evil, that is, the days in which disasters and trials come. There are no evil days, but he means days that bring him troubles. For God uses these trials for his good, the purification of his soul, and his preparation for eternity.

49.2.3.en: 2- What should frighten a person in the days of evil, which means the day of judgment, is only that his iniquities and sins, for which God will hold him to account, compass his feet; therefore a person should repent of his sins and prepare for the day of judgment.

49.2.4.en: 3- The iniquity of my heels is the ancestral sin, the sin of Adam, which pursues me to the day of judgment, but through Christ the Redeemer I am freed from it in the water of Baptism. The iniquity of my heels is also the iniquities which I commit at the heel of my life, that is, the end of my life, and do not repent of; these condemn me on the day of judgment.

49.3.0.en: 6- They that trust in their wealth, and boast themselves in the multitude of their riches; 7- None of them can by any means redeem his brother, nor give to God a ransom for him:

49.3.1.en: The writer rebukes the rich for trusting in their money and boasting in it. It cannot remove their sins from them, or stop the trials that come upon them, and consequently wealth cannot redeem a man after death or guarantee him a happy eternal life. And a man, or an upright brother, cannot redeem his wicked brother, and the upright cannot give God a ransom for his wicked brother, but each one is judged according to his works.

49.4.0.en: 8- (For the redemption of their soul is precious, and it ceaseth for ever:) 9- That he should still live for ever, and not see corruption. Ceaseth: remains preserved.

49.4.1.en: The writer turns in his speech to the poor, the lowly and the despised, and encourages them that their souls are very precious in the sight of God, and that they will live forever and ever. They must live looking to eternity, and not to this short life with its misery, which ends quickly in death, so that they are not disturbed by the toils of this life, nor by death and the grave; for if their precious souls live with God He will glorify them and give them rest in eternity.

49.5.0.en: 10- For he seeth that wise men die, likewise the fool and the brutish person perish, and leave their wealth to others. 11- Their inward thought is, that their houses shall continue for ever, and their dwelling places to all generations; they call their lands after their own names.

49.5.1.en: 1- Death is seen by the wise, and they prepare for it by an upright life; but the fool, who has the information and knowledge of this world but is a fool in the spiritual life and immersed in lusts and the love of money, and likewise the brutish person, who does not understand the sciences of this world and does not know the importance of preparing for eternity, both of them, the fool and the brutish person, die and leave their wealth, and find no rest in eternity.

49.5.2.en: 2- The strange thing is that the fool and the brutish person have strange thoughts within them, for they believe they will live forever in rest and greatness; that is, their outward greatness in their houses and their fame, as they give their names to houses, streets, squares and cities in order to immortalize their names, and they believe that this will continue forever although it is passing. The conclusion is that money and fame in this world do not benefit in eternity.

49.6.0.en: 12- Nevertheless man being in honour abideth not: he is like the beasts that perish.

49.6.1.en: The writer continues here his speech about the rich man who was occupied with the lust of the love of money and gained honor among men because of his wealth; he declares here that he does not abide in honor, that is, honor does not follow him after death, but he goes to Hades and loses his honor, because he dies and is buried like the beasts, which represent animal lust, for they have no honor in eternity and do not live forever in the Kingdom.

49.7.0.en: 13- This their way is their folly: yet their posterity approve their sayings. Selah.

49.7.1.en: In this verse the writer declares that those who relied on their wealth, and likewise their descendants who imitated them and lived occupied with the lust of money, die and are buried without honor like the animals, as we mentioned in the previous verse. Then he mentions the word Selah, a musical note, so that the reader may contemplate the vanity of wealth and the honor of this passing world.

49.8.0.en: 14- Like sheep they are laid in the grave; death shall feed on them; and the upright shall have dominion over them in the morning; and their beauty shall consume in the grave from their dwelling.

49.8.1.en: 1- The rich who were occupied with the lust of money die and are buried like the beasts, as we mentioned in the two previous verses. And their portraits which they hung on the walls, and likewise their power and their glory during their life in the world, wear away and vanish after death, because they dwell and settle in the grave, that is, Hades. Then judgment awaits them, where God judges them. And the upright have dominion over them, that is, they judge them, because they lived in the world like them but feared God. By "the morning" he means early after death, that is, the judgment, when God shines with His light and takes the godly into the Kingdom, and casts the wicked into eternal torment.

49.8.2.en: 2- Those who were occupied with the love of money are shepherded by death, and lose all their honor, because they refused the care of God during their life, and left the commandments of God, and loved the world; therefore they face humiliation and disgrace in Hades after death.

49.9.0.en: 15- But God will redeem my soul from the power of the grave: for he shall receive me. Selah.

49.9.1.en: 1- The hope of the upright is that God will redeem them from Hades. Those who died in the hope of the expected Messiah awaited His redemption, which was accomplished in the fullness of time, and He redeemed them, brought them up from Hades and moved them to Paradise.

49.9.2.en: 2- The writer's faith in God appears in that he hopes for the redemption of Christ after he goes to Hades, so that He brings him up with the believers to Paradise. Then he ends with the word Selah so that the reader may contemplate the great redemption of Christ for those who believe in Him.

49.9.3.en: Do not be occupied with the lusts of this passing world, because they are perishable; and do not be disturbed if one of your material rights is lost, but be concerned first for your relationship with God, and keep your peace, looking to the heavenly glories in which God will compensate you for all that you lost in the world.

49.10.0.en: 16- Be not thou afraid when one is made rich, when the glory of his house is increased; 17- For when he dieth he shall carry nothing away: his glory shall not descend after him. 18- Though while he lived he blessed his soul: and men will praise thee, when thou doest well to thyself.

49.10.1.en: 1- Do not fear the rich who have great possessions and material power, for the glory of these rich is tied to their passing possessions, which they will lose by death, and so they become without glory, especially since they cared for money and relied on it to glorify them; for he says "the glory of his house," and not his glory.

49.10.2.en: 2- These rich have no other glory, meaning spiritual glory in their faith in Christ, and they also accepted praise from the hypocrites and the self-interested around them, who saw the rich blessing their souls, that is, indulging themselves in the various material lusts. By this these rich increased in deceiving themselves, and drew away from God.

49.11.0.en: 19- He shall go to the generation of his fathers; they shall never see light. 20- Man that is in honour, and understandeth not, is like the beasts that perish.

49.11.1.en: 1- This rich man, who was occupied with his wealth, the worldly lusts, and the praise of others, will leave all this and die, and join his fathers whose life he lived, occupied with the love of money, and he will enter Hades, where there is eternal darkness, the reward of his distance from God, the true light.

49.11.2.en: 2- The writer ends this psalm by saying that God gave honor to every person, and even increased His giving and honored the rich with many possessions, that they might use them in almsgiving to the needy. But in selfishness they kept them for themselves. And the ordinary person did not live as the image of God. Likewise those to whom God gave His knowledge, such as the Jews, and who did not use this knowledge to believe in Christ, all these die like the beasts, that is, they lose the heavenly glory and go to Hades and torment, just as the beasts have no heavenly glory.

49.11.3.en: If wealth is vain and passing, take care to use it for the glory of God; take what you need and use the rest in doing good. Do not be occupied, like others, with gathering money, and do not be attached to it, for it is only a means that helps you live, so that you may enjoy a strong relationship with God, until you reach your great heavenly place. God the Judge: "The God of gods, the LORD, hath spoken") ... v. 1) Introduction:

49.11.4.en: 1- Its writer: Asaph, who was the chief of the singers in the days of the prophet David, and was of the tribe of Levi, and was assisted by two of the chief singers, Heman the Ezrahite and Ethan the Ezrahite (1 Chr 15:19). He led all the companies of praise in the Temple on the holy feast days. He was called the seer (2 Chr 29:30). The sons of Asaph also served in the ministry of singing, and continued in their service after the captivity, for one hundred and twenty-eight of them returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:41). Asaph wrote twelve psalms, the first of which is this psalm, then the psalms (Ps 73-83).

49.11.5.en: 2- When was it written? It was written in the days of the prophet David, and he was speaking about the greatness of Jerusalem and her beauty, and perhaps he wrote it by the spirit of prophecy about Jerusalem after the division of the kingdom, specifically in the days of Hezekiah or King Josiah.

49.11.6.en: 3- This psalm tells us about God the Judge who will judge His people, and also the wicked, and about God's preference for worship of the heart, and not formal worship.

49.11.7.en: 4- The writer of the psalm directs our eyes to the importance of loving God and praising Him, and likewise of loving others and not judging them.

49.11.8.en: 5- This is a didactic psalm in which God speaks to direct His people to right worship.

49.11.9.en: 6- The psalm tells us about the first coming of Christ in the fullness of time, incarnate and coming forth from Jerusalem (vv. 1, 2), then about His Second Coming on the great day of judgment (v. 4), so this is considered

49.11.10.en: 7- This psalm is not found in the Agpeya.
